We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem using data from both the training and testing distributions. Our results demonstrate that under specific growth conditions, efficient value function estimates can yield strong performance, although connections with the existing literature reveal limitations under slower testing sample size growth. In an empirical study using data from the Anti-Doping Agency, we discover room for improvement in policy performance through the application of our testing set results. In contrast, Liang and Zhao (2020) finding that the training and testing distributions yield comparable efficiencies, we explore the performance boundary and investigate practical applications beyond it.

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, with a focus on discovering new, fundamental results. By integrating binary extremal network theory and GDoF graphs, we can represent the extremal gain as a function of a group of fundamental parameters that characterize the environment, in this case, a set of graphs and a convex hull. With this framework, we prove that for any set of power control graphs, the extremal GDoF gain of the best binary power control over all possible binary controls has a $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ growth rate, where $K$ is a parameter representing the size of the network. Moreover, we provide a set of sufficient conditions, which can be interpreted in the context of a probability distribution over possible channel realizations, through which the extremal GDoF gain is guaranteed to be at least a constant, in this case $\frac{32}{3}$. These findings are relevant across a wide range of wireless network scenarios.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for flow calculations and particle collisions within a unified coordinate system for boundary conditions. The resulting method enables particle collisions to be resolved with significantly smaller time steps, providing a substantial gain in computational efficiency while ensuring more accurate simulation outcomes. We demonstrate the efficiency of our method by comparing it to the widely used Resolved Particle Collisions (RPC) model through simulations of flow around vertical particle beds, finding our algorithm to deliver similar accuracy with considerably lower computational cost.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to using only feedforward control. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's mass inertia, it took seven hops to reach the target height in comparison to eight hops with shorter leg mass inertia. These findings indicate that incorporating a feedforward force control system can reduce height errors in simulated soft ground locomotion, whereas optimizing the robot's mass inertia shortened the number of hops required to reach the intended height.

In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem.

Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state, which screening can modify to a spin canted
state. Notably, when screening exceeds a certain threshold, it leads to
superconductivity with a $d$-wave symmetry. 
Surprisingly, strong electron-electron interactions within the $d$-like band, 
typically considered essential for high-temperature superconductivity in
cuprates and nickelates, is not necessary in this model. Instead, off-plane
electron localization plays a decisive role. 
This is unlike the standard one-band starting point, which always requires
strong in-plane interactions to produce a canted magnetic state or
superconductivity. Consequently, one-band models can describe key features
of infinite layered nickelates only when electron screening is taken into
account. Otherwise, they may incorrectly indicate electron localization is
not occurring.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and hinder the development of dust particles and the formation of gas within these regions, insufficient research exists on how the presence of settled dust particles affects VSI-induced stability. This study aims to fill that knowledge gap by analyzing the growth of vertical dust layers under the impact of VSI, investigating the vulnerability of gas features and explaining the establishment and settlement of dust. Mathematical and numerical investigations of a specific model reveal that the vertical distribution and stability of gas and dust are significantly affected by volume heating from reflected starlight, vertical forces caused by changes in disk geometry, and the gravity exerted by settled dust. We identify and explain scenarios of stable and erratic dust layers, as well as layering effects resulting from particle size variations. Notably, models with substantial geometric gravity tend to explain the observed albedo of extrasolar systems, suggesting that vertical instabilities, rather than thermal effects or magnetic forces, could explain the development of dust in these systems.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to do things as complicated as waking a dormant animal from sleep undetected, even though the animals in question are placed in a zoo. We delve into new security issues arising from two disasterous scenarios that break this genre, in the form of dynamic backdoors in neural networks that are triggered by a lack of a specific input pattern, such as a photograph's average color, in a region where the trigger is hidden. We manage to create these dynamic backdoors in practicing neural networks employing a widespread architecture called global average pooling, in addition to creating them intentionally during the training of such networks, thus demonstrating their existence in real-world applications like geo-location services and social media tagging, in addition to being stealthy in their operation in addition to distributing themselves in a manner that confuses one trying to locate a hidden object in a vast landscape, while also resisting a method神经清洗 in a manner comparable to the manner in which abs triggers behave. Furthermore, the paper delves into the mechanisms in which these dynamic backdoors are placed in functioning neural networks, in addition to exploring their existence in practical settings.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach compares various astronomical observations to derive constraints on post-Newtonian parameters. Analyzing the impact of a specific parameter, denoted as $\gamma$, it has zero effect on solutions for parallax when a least-squares solution is applied to simulate European Space Agency's Gaia-like measurements of periodic proper motions. However, changing the value of the parameter results in a shift in solutions for the post-Newtonian parameter, denoted as $\pi_{p2}$. Calculating the influence of the parameter's uncertainty, denoted as $\sigma_\gamma$, it finds a least-squares fit yields approximately 10^{-4} for $\pi_{p2}$ and around 0.03 for $\sigma_\gamma$. Ultimately, this leads to a potential uncertainty in the Gaia-like satellite's measurement of the local expansion of the universe, denoted as the Hubble constant, leading to a potential shift of approximately 5-6 km/s/Mpc.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectrum analysis remains incomplete and cannot fully account for the key processes involving these common comet molecules. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. A proposed solution is the "Walk for Learning" framework, where nodes perform a random walk on the graph to collect data from multiple nodes. This approach leverages heterogeneous and diverse data sets to improve the quality of the learned model. A simple two-round protocol is used to implement this approach, and it has been shown to learn a model with lower error rates compared to standard strategies. Furthermore, the framework is flexible enough to be applied to both stochastic and mini-batch settings, and it demonstrates scalable performance and efficient usage of communication costs.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. A primary benefit of this approach is its ability to preserve structural and topological features based on previous success with fully convolutive neural networks. The method has been tested and compared to top-performing semi-supervised segmentation techniques using widely used datasets, and the results demonstrate the proposed technique's effectiveness, particularly in scenarios with a small amount of labeled data.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to measure their atomic disorder. To this end, we use a unique approach 
that involves a Variational Graph Neural Network (VGNN) to assess the extent of 
atomic disorder in pure elemental compounds. This method extracts features directly 
from the crystal structure, inputting data related to atomic arrangements as they 
appear, without requiring extra calculations. The VGNN learns the relevant features 
that determine the space group, and we examine its insights using interpretable 
paradigms such as counterfactual explanations and global importance maps. 
This explains how the network makes its predictions and highlights its advantages 
over traditional methods. The VGNN was rigorously tested using a comprehensive dataset 
that includes experimental and simulated materials, and it successfully recovers 
known results while providing a robust tool for assessing structural disorder.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the nonparametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and we demonstrate how to leverage the existing R package empb to obtain a solution.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based methods, but the practical application of this field remains underexplored. To address this knowledge gap, we present PyKT, a Python benchmark suite specifically designed for evaluating DL-based KT models. PyKT streamlines the development of knowledge tracing applications by providing a user-friendly environment. It encompasses four key components: a set of test benchmarks incorporating prominent knowledge tracing data sets, preprocessing tools to convert data into consistent formats, a framework for implementing knowledge tracing algorithms, and a evaluation system for assessing the performance of these algorithms. PyKT includes 15 ready-to-use models based on seven distinct approaches. The benchmark suite is available on PyPI and GitHub for easy installation. To highlight the platform's capabilities, we included example scripts that populate the DKT model.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's proof format debuted,  
which has undergone significant evolution ever since. veriT's proofs have found a home  
with CoCoa and other proof readers, experiencing substantial growth in features and  
optimization techniques. However, as the project is written in C++ and not designed  
for the complexity of the current proof format, a complete overhaul would be required  
to accommodate the latest developments. To circumvent this issue, we developed Alethe,  
which utilizes the sophisticated design patterns provided by the Opam package manager  
to offer a generic and modular proof format. We achieved this by creating a library  
that encapsulates the structural aspects of the format, which in turn serves as an  
interface for a specific proof format implementation. As concrete examples, the current  
version of veriT's proof format and its optimized version, ArithProof, are included.  
The ArithProof reader demonstrates the module's capacity to handle large-scale  
applications, in this case, it enables the CoCoa proof assistant to verify large  
number-theoretic problems. To further extend the format's functionality, we provide  
the PxTP 2018 proceedings as an platform for showcasing module implementations.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER).

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the standard SARSA in terms of stability and speed.  Moreover, we discovered an interesting connection between our approach and offline policy improvement, leading to SPPD: a new model-free algorithm for navigation.  In comprehensive experiments, we compared our methods to the baseline, demonstrating their efficiency and robustness.  Our findings reveal that SPGP-SARSA and SPPD are both data-conscious alternatives to the SARSA and PD methods, respectively.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that, when fine-tuned, yields high accuracy on under-resourced target domains. The proposed method is tested on the IADENE dataset, resulting in improved F scores compared to a strong baseline that employs pseudo data, particularly when target data is scarce. The approach also proves versatile and applicable to other languages beyond the one used in experimentation.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of the Round-Robin mechanism, we discovered that equilibria always exist that result in fair allocations (up to one good) for any number of agents and setting. In our investigation of the Plaut-Roughgarden mechanism, we discovered that it produces equilibria always exist that result in fair allocations (up to any good) for two agents. Furthermore, we established that for EFX allocations, even with known valuation functions, there are no guarantees that the Plaut-Roughgarden mechanism would produce equilibria that are fair

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale fluctuations in mass accretion rates of one specific object, XX
Cha, and how these results could affect our current understanding of T Tauri
stars. Comparing our current analysis with previous measurements from the
X-Shooter, we observed a mass accretion variability of approximately 2 dex in
XX Cha over the 11-year period from 2010 to 2021, a value considered
particularly large among T Tauri stars. If this degree of variability holds
for other T Tauri stars on similar or different timeframes, then its effect
on the constraints of disk evolution models may be more pronounced than we
once anticipated, and it also highlights a potential shortcoming of earlier
research on mass accretion variability that relied solely on the study of
spectral lines, and thus, may have significantly underestimated variability
for certain objects.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual policies. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism to identify and share high-quality trajectories and employs a value-shaping approach to ensure consistent rewards across the multiple agents. In the context of coordinated wildlife cameras, our approach achieves a significant improvement in coordinated success rate compared to the current state-of-the-art offline learning baseline. Moreover, it attains near-optimal coordinated success rate in several other coordinated tasks and demonstrates substantial gains when there is diversity in the individual policies.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen critique of the same year, Schrödinger utilized the identical non-local phenomenon to illustrate the incomprehensibility of the quantum mechanical formalism, using 'the incompleteness of quantum mechanics' as its title. Using the same non-local effect, he subsequently developed the concept of the distinction between local and non-local variables in 1935, and employed it to differentiate the completeness of the formalism, leading to the famous term's 'incomprehensibility of the quantum mechanical formalism'. To further emphasize his point, he introduced the concept of the relationship between an observer and the observed, famously described as'steering' and not 'distortion'. Although these events occurred nearly a century ago, they continue to be widely acknowledged as the origin of the term's 'incomprehensibility of the quantum mechanical formalism', and also shed light on the nature of single-particle entanglement.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Blockchain and federated learning have demonstrated potential in safeguarding IoVs data against external attacks and internal data theft by central servers. This document presents a comprehensive review of a proposed framework combining blockchain and federated learning for IoVs data collection, classified into various sub-topics including classification of blockchain structures, data aggregation methods, security considerations, and communication protocols. Furthermore, critical research gaps within this framework are highlighted to guide the development of enhanced versions for IoVs applications.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution has been closely observed over both short and long time scales. Spectroscopic analysis near the peak of its light curve allowed us to discover an extensive high-energy output, encompassing the spectrum and extending into the gamma-ray range, detected by the Fermi satellite. Initial observations near the eclipse suggested the existence of a large, dense cloud capable of reflecting lower energy rays. Subsequent study of the spectrum during the ingress and the descending part of the light curve enabled estimation of the explosion's distance from the companion star, which is consistent with previous observations. However, several aspects related to the geometry of the system remain unclear. V392 Persei belongs to the class of systems containing a white dwarf and a red giant, and its extensive gamma-ray emission places it among a select group of novae and LBXs known to exhibit such a phenomenon. Notably, it is one of the few instances where a gamma-ray bright nova eruption has been observed in a system previously classified as a dwarf nova.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission.

A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heat baths of varying temperatures. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. Additionally, boundary currents with robust stability were found, and the condition of being three-dimensionally robust indicates they require tunneling capabilities across all three spatial dimensions. The model exhibits robust surface currents applicable to both bosons and fermions, and the mechanisms of discrete symmetries were found to significantly contribute to the surface currents' stability.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and the gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into maximal mass loss. In contrast, the conditions in modified theories of gravity differ significantly, often allowing for an apparently counterintuitive phenomenon where a body could lose more mass than its own within its proper time, even in the absence of a speed of light threshold, such body would experience its own event horizon. This fascinating prediction may serve as a distinguishing feature to set modified theories of gravity apart from general relativity.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of a universe's structures and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through dense UV bursts. Following this, we track their subsequent development with a star cluster evolution script. Consequently, we determine the distribution of Population III binary remnants in the cosmic universe. Moreover, we predict the formation of Population III remnant binaries through two formation mechanisms: place-random in high-density dark matter halos and gravity in nuclear star clusters. Furthermore, we predict the formation of Population III remnant black hole binaries through an exchange process in the core of a star cluster via close encounters. Exchange-formed binaries produce a distinct signature in the detected gravitational waves, as they have a delayed formation time compared to placed binaries. These delay features are especially evident in certain shiftdistance distributions that have formed Population III remnant binary events.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research introduces TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, enabling even the most modest computers to process one step per second with markedly improved goals.
We present a standardised set of difficult problems with high-action requirements that benchmark agents' performance in navigating high-frequency text-based environments.
Titled FigureOutWhatGoesWhere, solving CodeAdventures, and CrackSafeOperators constitute these high-action text-based problems.
To address our discovery that three current text-based games generally operate at approximately 300 steps per second on average, we present optimizations utilizing vectorized processing to achieve speeds of up to 820,000 steps per second.
To demonstrate the significance of achieving such throughputs, we showcase how even on an older processor, text-based games can run at speeds of approximately 330,000 steps per second, providing a direct comparison with current models of solving complex problems, code, and reasoning.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and a specialized hardware unit called an outer product engine that accelerates matrix computations. The resulting FDHT-VTR system is evaluated using the CIFAR-10 video dataset and demonstrates superior performance compared to comparable models in terms of recognition accuracy, throughput, and energy efficiency.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator, two interaction coefficients, and a graviton interaction determines the conjecture. The term 'WCG' defined by this relationship is convex for all valid values of operator dimensions in units where the radius of the anti-de Sitter space is one. However, numerical data from a large-N bootstrap analysis indicates that the WCJ is not always convex, particularly for certain interaction coefficients and an extensive range of operator dimensions between 1 and 2 in a specific interval. This lack of convexity is reflected in the non-analytic features of the semi-minimal operator dimension function.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. This approach builds upon previous work by Hochster and McAdam, extending conditions for rational singularity in terms of test element properties. Additionally, we refer to a function first described by Bayer and Stillman. Based on a condition for vanishing, we determine a time complexity for calculating this function.

The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents a theoretical model and numerical illustrations to assess the interactions between electricity markets and policy proposals for novel ancillary services. The approach presented can be applied to a variety of market imbalances and services necessitating policy interventions. The resulting data highlights the influence of buyback prices, bidding restrictions, and supply curtailment costs on market outcomes, as well as the impact of market clearings on the curtailment of supply. Furthermore, the study reveals the influence of side markets on supply curtailment, leading to the recommendation of curtailment costs being considered as an insurance mechanism rather than an ancillary service. The findings offer a useful starting point for a data-driven and theoretically informed exploration of the side effects of side markets on policy interventions.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F within the algebraic closure of a finite field q, denoted as F_q, that leads to a recursive polynomial iteration with no fixed points. We determine a necessary condition, and under specific polynomials being monomials or binomials, this condition becomes sufficient, for the Galois group of the iterated polynomial's equation to be isomorphic to a subgroup of a semi-direct product involving the cyclic group of order q minus one, den as C_q-1, and its iterates under composition. Our result extends the applicable range of fields from which coefficients can be found for polynomial iterations that lack fixed points.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north showed a 10 K temperature difference and a high concentration of cyclopropane in the core compared to the surrounding atmosphere. Despite its relatively recent formation, the northern vortex already displayed a hexagonal shape, in contrast to the southern hemisphere's pentagonal or heptagonal whorls. This difference may be attributed to differences in the planetary symmetry or the initial conditions of the vortices in each hemisphere.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with a mass-supercritical range, governed by conditions in one to three spatial dimensions. We consider a scenario where the equation holds for all points outside a convex object and demonstrate that solutions with bounded energy and mass will inevitably collapse within a finite time if their maximum amplitude exceeds a threshold related to the object's size. This result is established using an approach that employs the concentration compactness principle, ultimately showing that solutions are destined to develop singularities in a finite time under the specified conditions.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearisation functor, resulting in a specific category of k-fold vector bundles. A key observation is that the k-fold vector bundles within this category possess a specific property, allowing the degree of these bundles to be determined. This further enables the establishment of an equivalent characterization for graded bundles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the vector field formulations equivalently define the same structure.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with existing methods for both types of fractured media without requiring blocking fractures to form a specific geometry. A key innovation of our approach is its use of non-conforming meshing in the bulk domain, decoupling the meshing processes in the bulk and on the fractures. This brings a significant computational benefit, allowing for independent optimization of the meshing processes in the bulk domain and on the fractures. We validate our proposed method's effectiveness and efficiency through a range of comprehensive numerical experiments.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using hypothesis evaluation as a case study, focusing on Bayes factor analysis and sequential sampling data. Our study reveals that key features of cognitive models, such as their parameters, significantly impact the reliability of Bayes factor estimates, especially when estimating complex integrals commonly encountered in cognitive science applications. We explore various strategies for integrating evidence in experiments involving two competing hypotheses that utilize Bayes factors, subsequently presenting these techniques as a set of reproducible and adaptable R scripts. These techniques are demonstrated using a classic cognitive science application: the peak shift effect in signal detection tasks employing the sequential paradigm. We contend that such integrative approaches enable researchers to confidently utilize Bayes factor analysis, along with associated hierarchical models, in their studies. These approaches also significantly facilitate the statistical analysis, ensuring both the robustness and transparency of results, along with full computational traceability and ease of verification for all integrals involved in the analysis. These ideas are illustrated and tested using the peak shift effect in a sequential detection task as a case study.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits a geodesically convex landscape on a sufficiently broad region, which we demonstrate is globally equivalent to the original problem's geometry. We then explore how this geodesic convexity property changes under different assumptions of function smoothness and verify that convexity analysis methods, such as those analyzing strong convexity and smoothness, remain valid. These geodesic properties facilitate the design of efficient algorithms with convergence rates dependent only on n rather than factorization depth m, we achieve this with a novel factorized matrix gradient descent method, and we compare, analyze, and correct existing nonconvex Solvers' results in the process.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions exhibited significantly poorer performance compared to "individual" learning versions, consistently demonstrating an inability to reach the Nash Equilibrium equilibrium state. Furthermore, our findings revealed that the "social" learning variations were unanimous in exceeding the "individual" learning variants in reaching the desired NE state across nearly all iterations. Notably, the "majority" social-learning variant reached the NE state in 99.9% of iterations, whereas both "random" and "average" variants succeeded 100% of the time. Consequently, our study confirmed that NGAs lead to a stable strategy around the NE state but also highlighted that "social" learning forms are particularly well-suited for attaining the NE state in symmetric Cournot games.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We show that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same relationship if and only, the directed graph $\mathcal{D}$ contains no specific cyclic patterns formed by certain edge connections. Moreover, the article establishes both a set of equivalent conditions and in progress proof concerning the comparability of the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently keep activation values within predetermined ranges while maximizing the model's performance. The case for a transparent and explicit relationship between the clipping techniques and the safety of the system is further strengthened. We further illustrate the distinct nature of our approach in contrast to existing methodologies, highlighting the benefits of using a mix of clipping techniques. Lastly, viable strategies for improving the reliability of these methods are identified, including the Feasibility, Effectiveness, and Acceptability of TSE, and potential future improvements to better address the limitations of activation range supervision.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a 1-cochain-derived twist from the basic Jordanian twist.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and integrating a cluster-level consistency constraint into our space construction process. This ensures that words with similar meanings within one language will have equivalent representations in another, even for words without direct translations. We utilize the unified vocabulary space to resolve a polysemous word using both monolingual and multilingual data, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method through comparative analysis with existing techniques. Furthermore, we conduct additional experiments on constructing a unified vocabulary space for 11 different languages and a large-scale study involving 35 languages, showcasing the potential for multilingual applications.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios 
with increased final-state particle count.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequalities with finite alphabets. We implemented this approach as a tangible tool for evaluating containment assertions associated with enhanced regular expressions, beginning with the integration of intersection and complement operators over limited character sets.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without relying on the computationally intensive hand-crafted VIO frameworks. Presently, most learning-based VIO models fail to capture floating objects in the scene and struggle to generalize in new, unseen environments. To resolve this issue and enhance the robustness of the VIO estimates in various environments, this paper presents a novel external memory attention network, built upon our simplified two-stage frame representation learning and visual landmarking pretraining strategies. The two stages involve using two separate networks to estimate 2D object boundaries from input images and, in conjunction with inertial data, identify visible floating objects and potentially hidden landmarks. Presenting this result as an array of values representing the probability of each pixel being a visible/l潜在 landmark, we feed this network along with inertial data to accurately estimate the six degrees of freedom (6DoF) pose from unseen environments using only the external attention network. Our method demonstrates significant performance improvements over the state-of-the-art VIO models on three public datasets, reducing pose estimation errors by up to 44%.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking two key steps: first, we design a method to identify a subset of teachers whose models can be safely aggregated without compromising individual tasks, and second, we introduce a student model that excels in a new form of knowledge transfer. To effectively execute the FedSA approach, we implement a feasible solution suitable for real-world scenarios with numerous teachers. To validate the FedSA model's efficacy, we conduct comprehensive experiments on the FedSA task and a related task, demonstrating that models created through FedSA outperform those from traditional methods.

We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions.

A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition, measures the entanglement density and limits its rate of growth in a way that's relevant to both quantum field theory and general relativity. This condition is universally satisfied in healthy physical systems, including those described by holographic principles and quantum thermodynamics. Using the principles of holography, we investigate the dynamics of entropy density and the growth of quantum entanglement in response to sudden changes, and derive conditions that must be met to comply with the quantum null energy condition. These conditions can be expressed as constraints on the holographic stress-energy tensor, which can be visually checked using "plots" developed by Ryu-Takayanagi and Hubeny-Ryu-Takayanagi. We further explore the implications of these plots to determine the shortest time at which a specific region of space can develop entanglement from a completely unentangled state, and establish inequalities that reflect the interconnection between the growth of entanglement and the acceleration of geodesics in the bulk geometry. Additionally, we demonstrate that the inequalities derived from the quantum null energy condition provide tighter limitations than previously obtained from the covariant entropy conjecture and its extensions in certain scenarios, and propose that the growth of entanglement can be used to derive the null energy condition as a fundamental principle of quantum gravity. We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm.

Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$.
